issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: Kofi had always been a man who lived life on his own terms. As a renowned dancer in his youth, he would spin and leap across stages with an ease that left audiences gasping. Even after retiring from the spotlight, Kofi remained active, teaching dance classes to children and performing at local community events. But all of that changed one fateful night when Kofi was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The accident itself was a blur, but Kofi remembers feeling like he was tumbling through space, unable to control his body or the world around him. He recalls seeing fragments - a shattered windshield, twisted metal, the sound of screeching tires - but the events leading up to and following the crash remain shrouded in uncertainty. When he tries to deliberately recall that night, Kofi finds himself grasping at wisps of memory, only to have them slip through his fingers like sand. In the months since the accident, Kofi has become increasingly withdrawn. He avoids going out, fearing that every car that whizzes by or every loud noise might signal another catastrophe waiting to happen. When he does venture out, he insists on standing with his back against a wall, where he can see everyone and everything around him - a habit that's earned him more than a few curious glances from strangers. Even social gatherings with friends have become minefields; Kofi is convinced that they'll ask questions or offer condolences that will force him to confront the trauma head-on. As a result, Kofi has isolated himself from his former social circle, too afraid of being asked about the accident or how he's coping. His reluctance to engage in conversations about the crash extends even to therapy sessions - whenever the topic arises, Kofi quickly changes the subject or cuts off discussion altogether. What frightens him most is the prospect of reliving that night all over again. At home, Kofi finds himself perpetually on edge, waiting for something to go wrong. Delays in his daily routine send his mind racing; when a bus doesn't arrive on schedule or a phone call takes longer than expected to connect, Kofi assumes the worst - another disaster lurking just around the corner. Every unexpected noise - a slamming door, a car horn blaring outside - sends him scrambling for cover. Kofi's lost faith in himself and his body. He can no longer trust that he'll make the right decisions or react quickly enough to avoid danger. The world has become an unpredictable, menacing place where institutions that should have protected him failed miserably. His own dance studio, once a sanctuary of movement and expression, now feels like a potential trap - one misstep could prove disastrous. Six months after the accident, Kofi's isolation is beginning to take its toll. His physical health has begun to suffer; his joints ache from disuse, and his usually sharp mind feels foggy and unreliable. It was only when he realized that he couldn't teach even a simple dance routine without freezing up in fear that Kofi finally sought help. As he sits in the therapist's office, fidgeting with the hem of his pants, Kofi is most afraid of confronting the memories he's been trying to keep at bay. But he's also desperate for some semblance of normalcy - to dance again without fear of collapse, to reconnect with friends and family without being held hostage by anxiety. Most of all, Kofi wants to trust himself once more, to know that his body won't betray him when it matters most.
